scaleInfo.name: Mixolydian Mode
scaleInfo.character: Dominant, bluesy, rock-friendly major with attitude

relativeScale.name: Major Scale
relativeScale.intervalDistance: Perfect 5th above the major root (G Mixolydian = C Major)

keyExamples.notes: G - A - B - C - D - E - F - G
keyExamples.commonUse: Most common mixolydian key, parent scale is C major, perfect for blues and rock

keyExamples.notes: A - B - C# - D - E - F# - G - A
keyExamples.commonUse: Popular rock key, great for classic rock and blues improvisation

keyExamples.notes: E - F# - G# - A - B - C# - D - E
keyExamples.keySignature: 3 sharps (F#, C#, G#) with D natural
keyExamples.commonUse: Natural guitar key, perfect for open position blues and rock

keyExamples.notes: D - E - F# - G - A - B - C - D
keyExamples.commonUse: Country and folk applications, comfortable open position fingering

patterns.description: Perfect for blues and rock in the key of G. Root on 6th string 3rd fret, flat 7th easily accessible.
patterns.fretDiagram: Open strings and first 3 frets, strings 6-2

patterns.description: Rock and blues favorite, moveable pattern starting from 5th fret on low E string
Country and folk applications, comfortable for fingerpicking and hybrid picking

commonPositions.usage: Rock solos, blues improvisation, all styles
Higher register playing, jazz contexts, lead work

diatonicChords.function: Tonic - Home chord with dominant character
Subdominant - Strong major chord, standard resolution target
Dominant - Minor dominant (unlike major scale's major V)
Submediant - Minor chord for emotional color
Subtonic - Characteristic mixolydian chord, defines the mode

commonProgressions.name: Mixolydian Shuffle (I-♭VII)
commonProgressions.description: The signature mixolydian movement - the flat VII chord gives the blues/rock feel that defines the mode

commonProgressions.name: Rock Mixolydian (I-♭VII-IV)
commonProgressions.description: Classic three-chord rock progression using the characteristic flat VII, common in Southern rock and jam music

commonProgressions.name: Blues Mixolydian (I7-IV7-I7-V7)
commonProgressions.description: 12-bar blues framework where mixolydian provides the scale choice for each dominant 7th chord

commonProgressions.name: Country Mixolydian (I-IV-I-♭VII)
commonProgressions.description: Country-style progression highlighting the mixolydian flat 7th movement, open and earthy character

genreApplications.usage: Essential for blues guitar, providing the scale for dominant 7th chord contexts and 12-bar blues
Classic rock guitar solos and Southern rock progressions with a bluesy edge
Country guitar licks, runs, and fingerpicking patterns with a dominant flavor
Dominant 7th chord soloing, V7 chords in ii-V-I progressions, chord-scale theory
Extended modal improvisation and groove-based playing over mixolydian vamps
examples: Fire on the Mountain - Grateful Dead

practiceExercises.name: G Mixolydian Scale Runs
practiceExercises.description: Practice the G mixolydian scale ascending and descending, focusing on the flat 7th that defines the mode
instructions: Start slowly with metronome at 60 BPM
Focus on the flat 7th note (F natural in G mixolydian)
Compare with G major to hear the difference
Gradually increase tempo as accuracy improves

practiceExercises.name: Dominant 7th Emphasis Drill
practiceExercises.description: Emphasize the flat 7th interval to hear and internalize the mixolydian character over dominant 7th chords
instructions: Play the root to flat 7th interval repeatedly from different scale degrees
Listen for the dominant, unresolved quality of the flat 7th
Practice over a G7 chord to hear the scale in harmonic context
Experiment with bending into the flat 7th for blues expression

practiceExercises.name: Blues Rock Lick
practiceExercises.description: Classic mixolydian blues rock phrase combining scale runs with idiomatic bends and rhythmic variation
instructions: Play over a G7 or G-F-C backing track
Focus on rhythmic feel and groove, not just notes
Add bends, slides, and vibrato for expression
Practice connecting this lick to pentatonic patterns

practiceExercises.name: Mixolydian vs Major Ear Training
practiceExercises.description: Compare mixolydian with the major scale to hear how the flat 7th creates the dominant, bluesy character
instructions: Play G mixolydian, then G major (Ionian) back to back
Focus on the 7th degree difference (F natural vs F# in G)
Notice how the flat 7th creates a less resolved, more bluesy feeling
Identify mixolydian in blues, rock, and country recordings

relatedScales.differences: Mixolydian has a flat 7th instead of natural 7th - this is the only difference
relatedScales.usage: Brighter, more resolved sound without the dominant edge

relatedScales.differences: Blues scale is a 6-note scale with flat 3rd, 5th, and 7th; shares the bluesy dominant character
relatedScales.usage: Perfect combination for blues guitar - mix mixolydian with blues scale licks

relatedScales.differences: Dorian is a minor mode with natural 6th; mixolydian is a major mode with flat 7th
relatedScales.usage: Sophisticated minor counterpart, works over minor 7th chords

relatedScales.differences: Lydian has a raised 4th creating a dreamy sound; mixolydian has a flat 7th creating a bluesy sound
relatedScales.usage: Dreamy, floating major mode used in jazz and film music

relatedScales.differences: Uses 5 notes from mixolydian (1, 2, 3, 5, 6), omitting the 4th and characteristic flat 7th
relatedScales.usage: Simplified soloing approach, can be extended to full mixolydian for more color

practiceRoutine.focus: Scale patterns and flat 7th sound recognition
